utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At the end of Friday's hearing, Mr. Karadzic asked to be allowed to further re-examine Ms. Hanson, in light of the Prosecution's re-examination in relation to the formation of the agencies and operation of them for the movement of population. The Chamber notes that the Prosecution, during re-examination, indeed, introduced new evidence regarding the existence and operation of crisis staffs and the agencies for the movement of population. However, this seems to have been triggered by the habit of unnecessary comments made by Mr. Karadzic on 14th of June, 2011, at transcript page 14641, regarding the implementation of population movement measures by these agencies, as Ms. Sutherland did, we took it to mean that such agencies actually were not established or were not in operation. The Chamber therefore considers that Mr. Karadzic can ask questions of Ms. Hanson in further re-examination, but only to the extent that they pertain to the existence and operation of the crisis staffs/agencies for the movement of population. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Can we look at P2723.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Further cross-examination by Mr. Karadzic:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, my question is this: The agencies, did they issue any kind of certificate or did they certify agreements on the exchange of property?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen certificates issued by these agencies. I believe I -- I note that in my report -- I don't have a copy of my report this morning. I don't know if it's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's coming. Thank you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was it that exchanged the property?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen many certificates of property exchange. What I have seen are people signing certificates to the -- to these committees that they are leaving voluntarily and that they are voluntarily donating their property to the municipality. As for the actual exchange, this one, yes, that we saw before, it says two people here, someone from Zagreb and someone from Banja Luka, exchanging apartments, is the example we have now. But I haven't seen as many of these as I have of the people simply signing their property over without an exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're talking about exchanges now. The agencies are for the purpose of property exchange, so among whom was the property exchanged?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this document, it's Bosiljka Njenjic from Zagreb exchanging with Fetah Kotari [phoen] from Banja Luka. In general, it was non-Serbs leaving and Serbs moving in, is my understanding of the general patterns. As I say, I haven't seen a lot of the exchange certificates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, it appears to be a Serb from Zagreb, Croatia. As I say, I haven't seen enough to claim a pattern, but, in general, Serbs from elsewhere who are moving into the territory of Republika Srpska, is my understanding. And if they're exchanging, then obviously it's someone who is moving out of Republika Srpska is exchanging with someone who's moving in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let's just agree on our terms. Did these Serbs flee? Are they refugees from these Muslim locations that are offering their property for exchange? Are they people who voluntarily left?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know enough. I imagine it's both. I imagine it's -- some are refugees from fighting, some are people who would rather live in Republika Srpska. In this case, it's someone from Zagreb, where there was no actual fighting, but apparently she preferred to live in Banja Luka than Zagreb for whatever reasons. I haven't seen enough to say -- I certainly don't know the individual's circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Why would somebody give away their property when there is an agency through which they can exchange the property? You keep saying that the property was given away. Do you know that on the 19th of August, 1992, I cancelled all of those decisions and that none of them was actually implemented?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said earlier -- last week, you said that you had cancelled those decisions. I was not aware of it then. You said it now, so I now know that you say that. I haven't seen a -- I don't -- if I saw such a declaration, I certainly would have changed -- well, I wouldn't have changed my idea of how much those declarations were signed under free will or not. I don't -- the reason why someone would sign such a declaration, give away their property, rather than exchange it, I believe they were moving out in such numbers, under considerable pressure to leave, that they felt the only way they could leave was to sign those certificates, but that is going beyond the scope of what I can actually show in this report. But I've seen many more, as I say, certificates donating property, supposedly voluntarily, than I have exchanges, and I've seen departures in such numbers that exchanges could not possibly be arranged for everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, were you stating the opinion on the influence of the central organs of power upon the crisis staffs? And if you did, why didn't you look at my decision of the 19th of August, in which I forbid such acts and cancel all of them that were signed before that date? It's a very important document. You don't have it, and you say you wouldn't change your opinion, regardless of new facts appearing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Karadzic raised this with Ms. Hanson earlier in his cross-examination, and he could have followed up with this question when he was dealing with the topic then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I tend to agree, but I consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your re-cross-examination is limited to what is new in her evidence adduced during the re-examination, so move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at P2725 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that those who wanted to leave had to pay transport costs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw that in one document that was shown in the redirect, and I have seen others. I don't -- some of the agencies, yes, demanded a fee for the -- even for signing the certificates. Yes, this is the document that here I noted they had to pay a fee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, this notice of where people are assembling and where they will be departing from, are you calling that the forcible transfer of the population? It states: "All passengers travelling on the convoy ..." And the time is announced where, and the account is stated where the money is to be paid. Does this amount to forcible transfer of the population?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]

Taken in totality with the documents and other information on the movement of population, this is certainly consistent with the stories we know of forcible transfer. This document, on its face, doesn't indicate one way or another. It does indicate the operations of this Agency for Population Movement, which is why, I believe, the Prosecution brought it to my attention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And what happened to those who did not pay for the ticket? Did you investigate that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was not one I looked at for my report, so I imagine in this case they didn't leave. But I can't do more than speculate on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those who did not pay for their ticket stayed and lived where they lived, and then we saw in Kotor Varos that money is being returned, even those who didn't take the bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that a comment or a question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that those who did not pay did not come to the bus, and those who paid and did not come to the bus, their money was refunded, as we saw in the case of Kotor Varos?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't know, on the basis of the documents I've seen, what exactly happened to those people, certainly not throughout the various municipalities. You did show me a document that said those who are not leaving will have their money refunded in Kotor Varos. Certainly, if this convoy is being organised from Banja Luka, there were non-Serbs in Banja Luka into 1993, so not everybody -- not all the non-Serbs left in 1992 from Banja Luka. utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, you will agree that in some cases, the municipalities asked for documents, among whom Banja Luka was the most liberal municipality, asking for just three documents. Some municipalities asked for as many as 10 documents in order for people to be able to leave. Does that sound reasonable to you, to ask for so many papers to be able to approve your departure? Does that sound like somebody was voluntarily departing or forcibly departing?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Asking for 10 documents in order to leave does not sound like simple rounding up and pushing them out. Of course, it sounds much more bureaucratic, more organised. But I don't know which municipalities you're talking about, if you're familiar which ones only needed three, which ones needed ten for departure. The voluntariness -- the voluntariness of their departure, this is one of those awkward places in my report where when I'm relying on only the documents of the crisis staffs, themselves, or their certificates, it is described as voluntary. I hope that there will be other evidence from other people that gives -- will explain to the Judges why I put "voluntary" in quotation marks. I think it's the totality of the events in the summer of 1992 that explains why these people departed. Once again, I cite Krupa as saying, Either you do it yourselves or we'll do it by military means. We see lots of evidence of the desire to be rid of non-Serbs in order to hold Serbian power in the territories claimed by the RS. We see Rajko Dukic in the assembly saying, I hope we've gotten rid of 60.000 Muslims from Birac. utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Dragan Kezunovic served as the chief of communications for the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the RS MUP, from its inception and throughout the 1992-to-1995 conflict. Before the war, he worked as the head of the Communications and Crypto-Protection Administration for the BiH MUP. Mr. Kezunovic was tasked by Mico Stanisic, the RS minister of the interior, to create a communications network for the RS MUP. The seat of the RS MUP moved from Vraca to Pale in April 1992. At Pale, it was first in Kalovita Brda, in an Energoinvest building. It later moved to Kikinda, also in Pale. In around December 1992, the RS MUP had a seat in Bijeljina, although the minister maintained an office and communications staff in Kikinda. The RS MUP contained both state security (RS RDB) and public security (RS RJB) branches. The RS MUP Communications Centre handled communications for both branches. The state security branch of the RS MUP was also entitled to use its own communications network. As in the pre-war network, RS MUP local police stations, SJBs, were connected to their regional centres, CSBs; the CSBs were connected to each other; and the CSBs to the republic-level RS MUP communications centre. The RS MUP Communications Centre at Kikinda worked 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. It had a backup electricity generator. Teleprinter operators worked in shifts and slept in the Kikinda building. Communications were sent and received using shortwave radio, ultrashortwave radio, radio relay, telephone, telegraph and fax. Communications sent by teleprinter were manually typed into the teleprinter, which encrypted outgoing and decrypted incoming communication. A digital communications system was used towards the end of the conflict. The RS MUP also made extensive use throughout the conflict of couriers who distributed communications by car. Acquiring equipment for the newly-created RS MUP was not difficult, as all existing CSBs and SJBs possessed teleprinters, other communications equipment, and backup electricity generators from the pre-war period. Almost every RS MUP police officer carried an ultrashortwave radio. There were some communications difficulties during the first few months of the RS MUP. These are described in the section co-authored by Mr. Kezunovic, of an RS MUP report concerning the first months of the RS MUP's operation: April to June 1992. Despite those initial difficulties, the report reflects the fact that there was always at least one form of communications link between the RS MUP Communications Centre and its subordinate CSBs. There were five such CSBs, and they were located in Sarajevo, Banja Luka, Trebinje, Bijeljina and Doboj. Mr. Kezunovic discusses several log-books and written communications which illustrate the functioning of the RS MUP communications system in 1992, as well as RS MUP communications documents relating to security arrangements for convoys containing President Karadzic and others in 1995. I would now like to call up, Mr. Registrar, please, 65 ter 16194A.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, on the screen in front of you, in a moment you'll see a document. I'll be asking you a couple of questions about that. If we could go to page 21 in B/C/S and 21 in English of that document, please. If we could focus in on the first entry in B/C/S, please. If you can see the first entry, Mr. Kezunovic, could you just explain what the first entry tells us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: This page is an excerpt from the records of telegrams -- or, rather, dispatches. As far as I can see, this is a record of the dispatches received. Most probably, it is the Public Security Station of Prijedor. Now, there is certain information contained in this document. I don't know if you're interested in that. There is the number, then the date; that is the first and second column. Then the third one is the time, and then the fourth one is the designation of that telegram, and then who this document comes from. For instance, the one in the first line is from the Bosanski Novi station. And then the next one is for who this is. That is marked by the number of the organisational unit involved. If I'm not mistaken -- well, the letters are very small, so I cannot really see this very well, but I think that it's the name of the document -- or, rather, the brief content of the document, and then you can derive the name of the document from there. Further down, I think you can see it better. In line 4 or 5, you can see that this is information, as it were. Finally, there is the signature of the recipient.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, you told us earlier that this appears to be a record of documents received by Prijedor SJB. And just as a general matter, looking at the "From "column, that's column 8, we see a reference to CSB Banja Luka in almost every entry. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This is, therefore, a record, is it, of communications from CSB Banja Luka, apart from the first communication, which is from SJB Bosanski Novi, to SJB Prijedor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could just turn the page to the next page in the English and the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Again, I would like you to scan just the column 8 showing the sender of all of the documents which are recorded here. Would you look at that, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Again, this is a record of a series of communications from CSB Banja Luka to Prijedor SJB; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you describe, in general terms, if you're able to do so, the method by which SJBs communicated with their -- with the CSB in their area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: You mean in general terms, not only in this period, but generally speaking, or do you mean by which means they communicated, or do you want me to describe this mode of sending and receiving written communication?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to you discuss the communication in general from SJBs to CSBs, and I'd like you to focus on the period after the establishment of the RS MUP.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, we tried to establish communication of all kinds; that is to say, speech and written communication. Of course, the possibilities were not the same everywhere. But specifically speaking, Prijedor and Banja Luka, that is where the system functioned, the one that existed before the outbreak of the conflict. That is to say, nothing changed there. There only could have been some small technical snags; for example, a power cut or damage on certain pieces of equipment, but that was redressed rather quickly. There was a system of telephone communications. Then also the coding system was in place, and coded messages could also be sent. That is to say that in all public security stations, we tried to make it possible to have telephone communication and written communications, either by teleprinter or telefax, depending on whether the messages were of an open nature or whether they needed to be encrypted, coded. As a reserve backup system, we had a system of shortwave radio stations that was used for the transmission of short messages, for the most part, because not all stations at first had the capacity or equipment to process written messages. It had to be done manually, and that is why more time was needed for the encoding process. Also, we had ultrashortwave radio that was used by the crime police and other operatives, whoever needed to move out in the field. At any rate, that happened locally on the territory of that public security station or CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kezunovic. Mr. President, I would like to tender that log-book which covers the year of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2744, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now like to call up 65 ter 11541, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If you would just look, Mr. Kezunovic, at the way that "Mico Stanisic" is written at the bottom of this document. Simply explain, very briefly, why it's spelt in this way.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That is because this telegram was typed out on a teleprinter, and on a teleprinter you do not have the letters "ch," "sh," "ch," "dj," et cetera. So, for example, "Ch" was written as two Cs, "Ch" as two Cs, if that's what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could tell us, just as a general matter, how a document signed and typed by somebody - for example, here Mr. Stanisic - would be communicated by teleprinter, just very briefly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: If we are speaking in general terms, that is to say, not about this specific document, but any document, it would first be typed up in an organisational unit, on a typewriter in the organisational unit where the document originated. Then it would be signed by the signatory, by the author. Then the document would be taken to the Communications Centre. Then it would be recorded by the communications operators in the log-book. If it is to be sent as an open message, then it can be sent by telefax or teleprinter, but without applying encryption methods. If it is supposed to be coded, then -- well, at any rate, it has to be re-typed on a teleprinter if it's to be sent by teleprinter. If it's to be sent by telefax, then it can be sent in its original version, as it was originally typed up. Also, the time is stated when it was handed over and who received it on the other side, and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. And is it correct that the teleprinted version of a communication normally would not contain the signature of the author?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: The signature of the author was on the original document that was brought to the Communications Centre, whereas this technical document, if I can call it that way, that is created by having it re-typed, because the operator has to re-type it from the authentic version into the teleprinter in order to be able to send it. Of course, there is no signature of the author on such a document. Only the name of the author is written, and then it means that it was signed in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: At the top of this document, we see that it's addressed to all CSBs and to all SJBs. Was it the general practice, would you say, for the minister to communicate directly to all SJBs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: It was up to him to decide who this document was to be sent to. That is to say, every author of a dispatch or any document that was being sent assesses who this document should be sent to. If it was the minister's assessment that it should be sent directly to all the public security stations and all the CSBs, and that goes without saying if it is written this way, not in some other way, it goes without saying that it's sent to the chief of the CSB and to all the chiefs of the public security stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2745, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I now have 65 ter 04817, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, this document here appears to be sent from Banja Luka CSB to a number of recipients. Could you describe, just briefly, who the recipients are?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Let us take it one at a time. "The MUP of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina-01." That means the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, 01, is -- I think it was the Police Administration. And 05, by way of information, I think that was the Analysis Department. Then the "MUP of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina - by way of information." So it is clear that in practice, there were cases when the same dispatch would be sent to several addressees. Some are supposed to take action on the basis of the document sent whereas the document was simply being copied to others so that they would informed as to what was going on and who communicated with who and for what reason. Then "Public security stations, to all," "the chief and the commander of the Milicija station," and then finally it also says, "Bosanska Grahovo, Bosanski Petrovac, Drvar, Glamoc, Kupres, Donji Vakuf, Srpska Bosanska Krupa, Srpski Bosanski Brod, to the chief."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, the reference -- the second reference to the MUP of the Serb Republic of BiH, where was that physically at this time, the 10th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Physically, it was in several locations, mostly in the area of Pale, and a part of the ministry was in Vraca, in the former Cadre Education Centre of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I would like to tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2746, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to call up now, please, 65 ter 21888, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You see, in this document, there is a reference to a daily incident bulletin. Do you see that, Mr. Kezunovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: If you can just zoom in a little bit. It's a little bit too small, the text that I'm to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If you can't see it, just say so, and we can put the English aside for a moment.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: It's all right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. Could you tell us what the daily incident bulletin is, insofar as you understand it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I will answer that question, but I don't see, in this document, that it says "Bulletin."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry. Just on the second line in the middle of the document, do you see the word "bulletin"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Ah, yes, I see it. "In view of the fact that the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is now located in Sarajevo... " They are thinking of Vraca. The 18th of April, I direct that the bulletin of daily events and other significant security information of interest be sent to this ministry by telefax. Yes, I can answer your question now, what the bulletin is. A bulletin is an information review of daily events which are of security interest, as we refer to them, regarding events that happened on the ground, in the broadest possible sense, in the field. Then the bulletins which, during the previous 24 hours, covered the events would be sent by Public Security Station officials and compiled into one report, which would be sent to their superior security centre, which put it all together into one report and sent it to the ministry, at the headquarters. And then the Information and Analysis Service would go over all the information and classify them according to their set system, and then make an overview of all those events, and that was the bulletin. It could also be a weekly bulletin, not just a daily one. But in the operative sense, a daily bulletin was something that was most efficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. And this communication is addressed, as we see, to the CSBs -- to all five CSBs of the RS MUP; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2747, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I have document 20636, please. Could we zoom in on the top left-hand corner of the document, please, the top third.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you describe what this document is, please, Mr. Kezunovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: This is one of those daily bulletins, a bulletin of daily events, number 3, specifically, relating to the 22nd and the 23rd of April, 1992. Do I need to comment on the contents?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No, that will do for the moment. Could I direct your attention -- there's no need to read the entire document, but we see a reference to events taking place in Sanski Most municipality further down that page. Could you simply tell us, which CSB area did Sanski Most fall under?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Sanski Most was part of the Banja Luka CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Further on in this document - perhaps we can turn to it - we see a reference to events taking place in Zvornik. It's on page 2 in the B/C/S and page 3 in the English. Which CSB did Zvornik fall under?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: In that period, it belonged to the Bijeljina CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: On page 4 in B/C/S and page 4 in English, we see a reference to events taking place in Brcko. Which CSB did Brcko fall under?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Bijeljina, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And, very briefly, Ilidza is also mentioned in this document. Which CSB region did it fall in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, in the previous document we saw Mr. Stanisic's order to report to the MUP in the form of a daily bulletin. But this document is a daily bulletin, written by Stanisic, addressed to whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you mentioned previously, Stanisic issued orders that the report should be sent to the ministry, based on which a bulletin was made. I don't know what happened to the bulletin after that, because the Administration for Information and Analysis was in charge of that. I don't know if it was sent to the ministry in order for events to be analysed, in order to - how shall I put it? - devise operative plans for orders and measures for action in the field. It could also have been used to inform any of a number of politicians, if any of them requested that at the time, but I doubt that anybody did because probably there was some kind of special list of persons to whom the reports were sent. From this, I really cannot see that this document was sent to anyone, unless there is another accompanying list or document that goes with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. This will be admitted as Exhibit P2748. Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could we call up 65 ter 08542, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: When this arrives on the screen in front of you, Mr. Kezunovic, we'll see that this is Daily Report 6, dated the 6th of April -- sorry, excuse me, the 25th of April of 1992. And if you look at the second paragraph, we see a reference to events in Prijedor. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, in the third paragraph in your version on the same page, on the next page in English, we see a reference to a case -- certain criminal offences taking place in Banja Luka, including the case of pick-pocketing or pocket-picking, as it's expressed in the English translation. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph. In Banja Luka, during the day, 16 crimes were committed; 11 break-ins, three vehicle thefts, two fuel thefts, and one pick-pocket theft. In one attempt, public order was disturbed by an unidentified person or unidentified persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Later on in this document, we see references to events in Bratunac municipality. Which CSB did it fall under at this time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not 100 per cent sure, but it was either Bijeljina or Sarajevo, one of those two, because organisation changed several times, in terms of which station would fall under which centre. This changed several times, so I cannot really say at that point in time, on that date, whether it fell under the Bijeljina or the Sarajevo centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: There are also references to Brcko and Zvornik. You told us already they were under CSB Bijeljina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, yes. Later, Zvornik at some point in time became a security centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2749, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we now call up, please, 65 ter 16186. And if we could go, please, to page 4 in B/C/S and page 4 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This is a document, Mr. Kezunovic, which you've already referred to in your amalgamated statement, and I want to draw your attention to a couple of the entries in it. If we could look at entry numbers 13 and 15 on the page in front of you. Perhaps for the moment, if we could put the English to one side and bring up the B/C/S only just for the moment. I want you to focus on the fourth column across, which indicates the addressees. And, first of all, could you just describe entry 13? What does it tell us, in brief terms; who it's from and who it's to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: It states that it's being sent by the B and H MUP under the number such and such. I don't have to read it. It's an addendum to a dispatch of 01/18/92 of the 20th of April regarding -- and this is something that I cannot read.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sorry. Just to clarify, Mr. Kezunovic, don't worry about the actual title of the document. I just want to focus on the addressees. We see there "Banja Luka 078," then "CB Sarajevo," "CB Bijeljina," "CB Trebinje," "CB Doboj"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Are those the five CSBs of the RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If you look at item 15, are the addressees the same five CSBs? And that's a communication of the 27th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same centres and the same telephone numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The signature in the extreme right column, could you just tell us what that should indicate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: This is the signature of the operative, the person who sent the dispatch. It's not the author of the document, but the communications person, the operator.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we move to page 6, please. Keep the B/C/S for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. Gaynor, the column of -- can we see the English page. What I meant to say is the column for addressees in number 13 should be identical to that for number 15, given the English translation is -- some part of the English translation is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. President. That is the case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we move now to page 6 of this document in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, on page 6 -- sorry, could we move to the next page, please. Just focus on item number 30. If we could blow that up, please. This appears to be a record of a communication on the 4th of May, 1992, addressed to the same five CSBs as well as to SJB Pale; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, and it writes -- it states here that the Sarajevo and Pale centres received it by messenger.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you look at entries 33 and 34. The recipients in 33 are described as "SSUP" and "MUP R Srbije," and in 34, the recipient is "SSUP." Could you indicate, in items 33 and 34, where are they located?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: This is the federal SUP and the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, and you can see that by the telephone numbers, by the area codes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we move to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If you could look at items 37 and 40. 37 refers to a communication on the 8th of May, 1992, to CB Banja Luka. Communication 40, first a communication on the 9th of May, 1992, to "B.L.," with "078 39-155." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I can see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do they appear to be records of communications to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a Banja Luka number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could move to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very briefly, items 42 and 44, dated the 10th and 11th of May, 1992, do they appear to be addressed to the same number in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: 42, yes. And what was the other number you mentioned; 44?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And we have two entries for the 11th of May, 1992. Both entries appear to be addressed to all five CSBs. Could you confirm that? Those are entries 47 and 48.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's for all five centres. But I cannot see the numbers for Doboj and Trebinje, which probably means that it was probably not delivered to them, because in earlier cases where we saw all five of them, we saw phone numbers for each of the five. Here, we don't have phone numbers for Doboj and Trebinje. I don't know what that means. Perhaps for some reason it was not delivered, perhaps because of an electricity cut or some other malfunction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This log-book, I think you've described it in your statement earlier, was one held by the RS MUP Communications Centre at Vraca; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: At that time, was the minister, Mico Stanisic, was he personally based at Vraca?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: In the sense that he spent more than a day there at a time, I don't recall that I met him at that building, in the office where all the people from the MUP were sitting, the chiefs of administrations and some departments, including myself. I saw him once, but it doesn't mean that he didn't come more than once. But I only met him, actually, once.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: During the period of the entries that we've been looking at, was there a separate Bosnian Serb MUP -- RS MUP communication centre in Pale?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a MUP communications centre in Pale. In the beginning, briefly, it was in the Energoinvest facility at Kalovita Brda, and then later it moved to a children's holiday resort from Kikinda, which is how it got its name, "Kikinda." That's where the MUP Communications Centre was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: So, briefly, this log-book that we've been looking at does not contain a reference to any communications that might have been sent during that period from Pale to the CSBs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't pay attention to all the documents, but I think that all the documents that are recorded in this record of received and sent dispatches from Vraca originated from people who were actually there, which doesn't mean that some document that was received there was not received in Pale at the same time. It could happen that it was received by the Pale Communications Centre and here as well, because both centres had the same weight as the Communications Centre of the ministry at the seat, because if there was a need for ministry people who were in Pale to be informed about something, it would be sent to them. I don't know if there was a technical possibility for them to receive it there. Perhaps those in Pale could receive it and those who were in Vraca could not, but that's another case. But, generally, this is how it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that document. I'd like to note for the record that in the amalgamated statement of the witness, he explains that the rest of this log-book is a record of communications from CSB Sarajevo. That's explained in his amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for our convenience, do you have the para numbers? In the meantime, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2750, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. This is explained at page 40 of his amalgamated statement, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I note the time. It's about time to take a break, if it is convenient, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It is, indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I could call up 65 ter 05046, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: As you'll see in a moment, this document is headed information on the daily events from 9th and 10th May, 1992, on the territory of Banja Luka. It is dated the 10th of May. If we could focus on the top of the B/C/S version, please. Mr. Kezunovic, I think you see a fax header and a stamp there. Would you be able to tell us anything about those?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: This is something that was not customary, to place a stamp later on and to register a document under a certain number within that stamp. Most probably this is a document that was received from someone. I say "someone" intentionally, because I don't know who it could be. So someone who received this document and registered it under this number and date within their own records. It is like when you hand in a document in a court of law or in the municipality or somewhere and then when they stamp your own copy as a receipt that they had received the same document but in the original. This was not the usual thing in terms of the documents that were exchanged in communication centres, but you can see here it says "Serbian --" I can't read the second word, and then it says "Bosnia-Herzegovina, Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In fact, could you help us with that. Where it says in the header to the left "Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ministry of the Interior, Sarajevo," was the Ministry of the Interior -- I think you've expressed this before, was it in fact based in the city of Sarajevo at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, one of the seats, that was in Vraca. I don't know up until which date it was in Vraca, but it could be treated as the seat of the MUP. Part of the MUP, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, the B/C/S version of this document in fact contains two versions, one of which contains the signature of Mr. Stanisic. We can look at it if you want, Mr. Kezunovic, but my question is this: This document contains information about events only on the territory of Banja Luka. It covers Sanski Most, Kljuc, Banja Luka, Prijedor, Bosanska Dubica, Bosanska Gradiska, Prnjavor, Bosanski Novi and Gornji Vakuf municipalities and it is signed by Mico Stanisic. Perhaps you could explain why or how Mr. Stanisic is in receipt of all of that information about events taking place in those municipalities.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a hard question, because he could have received this in several different ways. Most probably he received it by way of a dispatch, a report from Banja Luka about daily events in the form of a telegram or a dispatch. Again, not he but the analysis and information department, and then they wrote it up as an information on daily events. There's another possibility. If that was sent to the ministry -- from the ministry by someone else, then the minister was supposed to sign that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that document, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2751, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We'll take break in the documents for a minute, Mr. Kezunovic. The Trial Chamber has heard evidence of a meeting of the Bosnian Serb Assembly which took place in Banja Luka on the 12th of May of 1992, attended by, among others, Karadzic, Krajisnik, Koljevic, Plavsic, Mladic, and deputies from across many parts of Serb-held territory. Are you aware yourself of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I think that I wasn't aware of it and that I wasn't in Banja Luka at the time. That is why I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You've had a chance to inspect briefly minutes of that meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Those minutes are P135, for the record. Now, do you have any experience in your career both before the war and during the conflict with the security of major events attended by high-level dignitaries?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I had such experience before the war and during the war and after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you tell us just a little bit about the kinds of security arrangements that would have to take place within the MUP to co-ordinate the security for delegates visiting a city from other parts of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if necessary, I can give an example. For example, this Assembly session in Banja Luka, what measures would be taken for such an event. In the briefest possible terms, it involves everything that is the regular work of the Ministry of the Interior but with heightened intensity, and more people take part in the security operation, that is to say, more members of all services participate. Now, what does that mean? Security should be provided for such an event for as long as it lasts. If it's two days, then it's two days round the clock. If it's three days, then it's three days round the clock. Also, special measures should be taken in terms of physically securing the facility itself where that Assembly is being held, the building. Then the building or buildings where the MPs are staying -- or, rather, the dignitaries that are entitled to special protection under the law, for example, the president of the republic, the president of the Assembly, the prime minister. Then security has to be provided in traffic on such an occasion. If there is special regulation that is needed for such an event, then that has to be prepared according to a special plan. My role was to create a plan of communication for such a situation but for the needs of the security service, that is to say, so that all the services within the Ministry of the Interior could function properly. That would be it in the briefest possible terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you happen to know how delegates arriving from Pale and Han Pijesak made it to Banja Luka on the 12th of May, 1992? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I personally have no such information, but I think that it was only possible by air. It was impossible by land to reach Banja Luka from Pale. I assume that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you have experience with coordinating security for transport of dignitaries by air within the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have that kind of experience, because that is for air controllers. That is a different kind of security, namely whether the flight is safe and at what time it should take place and all these other elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now back to the documents, Mr. Kezunovic. Could I have 65 ter 05291, please. Again, this is a document signed by Mico Stanisic. It's dated the 17th of May, 1992, and it is addressed to the security services centres in Banja Luka, Bijeljina, Doboj, Sarajevo, and Trebinje. I would like you to look at the stamp at the top -- excuse me, the handwritten comments on the top right-hand corner of this copy, please, Mr. Kezunovic, and could you tell us anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Perhaps we could expand the top right-hand corner, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The comment is as follows: "Was not given to Doboj. Sent by courier on the 18th of May, 1992," and the signature of some person, probably an operator at the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the last sentence of the body of the communication we see Minister Stanisic setting out a dead-line for submission of reports, and he says: "Due to the content of reports --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let him see the sentence. Zoom out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It says: "Due to the content of the reports, send the reports by courier or coded with full guarantee of confidentiality of the information." Are you able to tell us which of the CSBs would have used couriers at this time which would have used coded communication?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I think that if there are no technical problems involved then everybody could have received this coded via teleprinter. However, as I said, if there were no technical problems at that point in time. As far as I can remember, during the proofing I explained this to you, namely that during 1993 -- so it was even worse in 1992, but anyway, in 1993 when I was transferred to Bijeljina, when the ministry definitely moved to Bijeljina, I was the last one to move. Every day there would be brief power cuts, 50 times or even more than that, which means that if you start transmitting a dispatch and if there's a power cut, you have to wait for electricity to come back again or to have the generators turned on and then to start all over the again. I'm giving you this example, but theoretically it could have been sent to all five addresses if there were no technical problems at that particular point in time, and I have no way of knowing that right now, and I cannot remember either.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, the handwritten comment at the top right says -- indicated it was sent by courier to Doboj. Do you see anything to suggest that it was sent by courier to any other of the CSBs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like to tender that, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 2752, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could we call up document 22932, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you see the number of this particular daily bulletin, Mr. Kezunovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And you'll remember that earlier on we saw a daily bulletin with a much lower number. I think it was number 6?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In this particular daily bulletin, we see reference to events described as being within the areas of the Sarajevo CSB and the Banja Luka CSB and the Bijeljina CSB. At the very end it indicates that Doboj and Trebinje did not submit their daily incident bulletins. Do you see those references?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see the last part where it says that these two had not submitted. That's what I don't see. The rest is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's on the next page, please. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The information collated in this document was collated in the same way as you've described earlier. Is that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I also have daily report number 107 from the 23rd of May, 109 from the 25th of May, 111 from the 27th of May. I propose in the interests of expeditiousness to tender those without showing them to the witness, but I'd just like to record that daily report number 107 refers to events in Banja Luka, Kotor Varos, Donji Vakuf, Prijedor, and Kljuc among other areas. 109 refers to events in Kotor Varos, Sanski Most, and Banja Luka. 111 refers to events in the municipality of Rogatica as well as the village of Kozarac in the municipality of Prijedor, and I'd like to tender those for admission. I can read out the 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Witness has confirmed the authenticity during the course of proofing. That's what you're suggesting. Witness has --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. He has looked at them and he agrees that these are part of the same series of daily reports issued by the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Kezunovic, or would you like to see them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Although in principle we don't believe that documents should be admitted without being shown to the witness, given their similarity to what he's just described, we don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that observation, we'll admit those three documents. We'll give the numbers for those.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The current document will be Exhibit P2753, and the three mentioned by Mr. Gaynor will be Exhibits P2754, P2755, and P2756 respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: My final question, Mr. Kezunovic, concerns the network of radio relay stations used by which the RS MUP. Could you explain to Their Honours whether the network of radio relay station which your service used was identical to or distinct from the network of radio relay stations used by the army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: The network of radio relay stations is actually a network of links, as we call them, between different points. This network that we used was the telecom network, that is to say, the public PTT company. A small capacity of theirs was used by MUP. And that has nothing to do with the radio relay stations of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just to clarify the transcript. It has nothing to do with the radio relay stations, the network, did you mean the plural, of the army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Radio relay stations are devices that are on hills at certain altitudes, and some centres are linked up that way, in big towns and elsewhere. So the radio relay network, the radio relay communications through one or more radio relay stations is actually just one type of link between these points that goes through the air. Another type of link are cables. So the same thing happens either via cable or via radio relay points, the very same thing. So the same communication can go via radio relay networks or via cable. Radio relays are just optically visible to one another, and then it depends on how many are needed between Sarajevo and Banja Luka, for instance, and that is how this communication is ensured. In principle, this kind of communication is a back-up for the cable system which is more secure and more stable. Radio relay systems are actually a back-up. And now the fact that it was simpler in technical terms to maintain this radio relay system in peacetime is a different matter. So most of the communication went that way. So what was used by the MUP was an integral part of these links, either radio relay or cable but that were owned by the telecom -- or, rather, the PTT as it was called at the time. The military had separate systems, cable and radio relay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kezunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That ends the examination-in-chief subject to the tendering of the associated exhibits. I'd like to tender all of the exhibits which have been listed in the notification for Mr. Kezunovic which have not already been admitted by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Robinson, do you have any observations?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't object, Mr. President, to any of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On a separate matter - excuse me, Mr. Gaynor - I forgot to ask you about your position in relation to the Appendix B in relation to Ms. Hanson. If you have any, the Chamber would be assisted by hearing you again on those issues, on those items.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: In general I don't have a need to discuss the specific items but in general we think the Chamber ought to stick with its position that it announced at the beginning of the examination which was that any documents that the Prosecution wanted admitted from Appendix B should be put to the witness and those that were not put to the witness we don't believe should be admitted by a bar table motion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If my memory's correct, please correct me if I am wrong, did you not say you objected to only one item when asked at the outset?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think at the outset I said that we prefer to have them all presented to the witness for her comment, and I pointed out and in specific there was at least one item we thought was objectionable because it was a newspaper article. So we didn't mean to waive our objection to the procedure which seems to have been that documents ought to be placed before the witness, and as illustrative of that I pointed out at least one document that we felt would not be appropriate for bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And that article is still included.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think that was withdrawn by Ms. Sutherland today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Forgive if me if I'm belabouring the obvious but I thought it necessary to point out that the discussion at the outset of the examination was not -- could not be simply characterized as the Chamber sticking to its position that any documents had to be put to the witness as we were -- as we noted, we were operating consistent with the specific guidelines of the Chamber in crafting appendix B but would endeavour to heed the Court's preference and present as many as possible to the witness while nevertheless preserving the existence of Appendix B pursuant to the Court's guidelines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll issue a decision in due course. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just want to clarify that the first daily report that I showed to Mr. Kezunovic was actually daily report number 3. That's P2748, not number 6, as I mentioned earlier. I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The associated exhibit will be admitted and given number by the court deputy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, now it's for you to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Kezunovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to express my gratitude for kindly meeting with the Defence and with me personally, and I hope that this will help us to present your knowledge in a focused way. During this interview, you confirmed that before the elections in the republican SUP you were called in the republican SUP, and you were told that the party organisation in state organs will no longer apply. Up until that time, did the League of Communists have the leading role in the organisation of institutions, including the MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Up until those elections, it did have its basic organisations in all state organs, and this is how it functioned up until these multi-party elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You told us that you were angry at the state organs because the state was falling apart. You left the party, and after that you did not join any other party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was: Party meetings were convened at the organisational entities. That's how it was organised. And we were told that from that point on, pursuant to a decision by some organ, I cannot remember which one, any kind of party organisation in the state service no longer applies and that we all needed to decide where we wanted to go in the field, and I demonstratively stood up at the time, you are correct, and said that the League of Communists was the one that was most to blame for the break-up of Yugoslavia. I ripped up my party booklet in two, handed it to the party secretary and I told him that I hoped the court and everybody I said that they could spit on my cheek if they see me at any party or that one again. Well, I don't know how things proceeded from there, what the people decided, who organised themselves in what manner. I don't know, and it's not important to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to know that I am waiting for the interpretation, and that is why I'm making these breaks. After the first multi-party elections in November 1990, did you remain at your post even though you were not a member of the Serbian Democratic Party and you did not know me personally?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I stayed at my post, my job. I was not a member of any party, and I was actually at that time the acting chief of the administration. According to the rules, I was the chief of a department, and as such I was the deputy of the chief of the administration since there was no chief of administration at the time. He was transferred to the city SUP. Later he retired, but at that point in time, I was acting chief of the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then in the interview with the OTP of the 8th of November, 2004, pages 7 and 8, this is 65 ter 22432, as well as in your testimony in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case, this is 1D356, page 1, page 102 and 104, you confirmed that the SDA primarily was the most persistent in appointing their people at MUP positions, bringing in numerous people who did not work in the MUP before then; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is so. First of all, the -- certain people were appointed to the key positions in accordance to their party affiliation who did not perform those jobs in the ministry if they were in the ministry already, and then people from outside of the ministry were brought in as well. Allegedly, I'm saying allegedly, because at the time I didn't know about these things, an agreement was reached among the parties how to divide the key posts among the parties. Specifically, I know that the minister was from the SDA, the deputy was from the SDS, the chief of the administration for personnel was from the SDA, and then for the second part of the answer I would say that it was quite characteristic for the situation at the time that Hilmo Selimovic was appointed to execute those jobs as an SDA cadre. And what else became characteristic in general, after those elections, as far as the relations inside the MUP were concerned, there was no longer any mutual co-ordination or mutual information exchanged about common matters relating to the ministry, including the personnel policies as well. So the chief of the personnel administration simply, as far as I know through my administration, basically what happened was that, I'm so-and-so. I don't know where I've been before that. Where is my new chair? That is how people were being brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. First of all, our usual manner and usual practice in multi-ethnic Bosnia is something that I would like to clarify. During the Communist times or socialist times, was it not a habit to appoint somebody from one ethnic community as chief and then his deputy would be from the other ethnic community simply in order to control each other and so that their work, that of one or the other, could go through democratic checks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was in practice, and care was taken, as far as I can remember. It wasn't just a pure formality. It was something that thorough agreements were reached about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You remember that after the elections these posts were divided in such a way so that if the chief was a Muslim the deputy was a Serb, or if the Serb was the chief, the deputy would be a Muslim or a Croat, and that these were divided among the three victorious parties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That is how the whole story went. As far as those of us who were actually doing the work, this is what we were told, that everything would be balanced out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this Selimovic, am I correct when I say that this Hilmo Selimovic who was brought in as the chief of the personnel service was a party member from the hard-core SDA party who came to the MUP from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the Serbian side, the Serbian Democratic Party, did it nominate Vito Zepinic as minister, who was a professor at the police school, the police academy and was not a member of the SDS for that post?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, that's what was said, that he would be deputy minister. As for whether he was a member or not, that's something that I don't know. Many at the time said that they were not members, but they turned out to be. For many of them, there was talk that they were not members, but then in the end it turned out to be that they were. So I don't know whether he was a cadre of the SDS or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, as far as you're concerned, you confirm that you were not a member of the SDS and that we were in favour of you staying at your post because of your expertise, and that post was allocated to the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, and had it not been that way, I would have been removed a long time before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You described that in the Stanisic case. This is 1D3596, Stanisic transcript pages 14 and 15, and again pages 101 and 102, where you describe that a new administrator, Akif Sabic, suddenly turned up who told you that you were to look for a new job; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is just a brief telling of that story. I don't know how long I was acting official in that post, and then just one morning this Akif Sabic turned up. He -- Hilmo Selimovic called me to his office. This other guy was sitting up there with him, and he told me this is the new chief of the administration, introduce him to the work, through all the organisational units, show him his office, and where his posts are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. And when you showed him the ropes, then after a certain period of time he told you that you were fired from the service; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, actually, there is one other period, which is the period during which I was quietly excluded from certain activities so that even some very ordinary simple tasks from my department were not given to others as tasks by me but were given by someone else. This couldn't have been done by this Sabic because he wasn't that familiar with the organisation and the manner of work, especially not in the way that we did the work but it was some other associate from the administration that probably did that, telling them what they were supposed to do, and then it all culminated in me being summoned one day and being told that I have an hour to find a job and to tell him where it was exactly that I had found this job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that he felt that you did not accept your marginalisation? Did you sense that, and did he sense that you had not accepted that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was absolutely sidelined. You could see that in all manner of ways. Simply when I went to the workshops where the workers were, if they were talking, this would suddenly stop. They would stop talking about the work in front of me, meaning that I was not fit to hear what they were talking about, even though in a way I was a superior to all of those workers. And there was a situation in which the only thing that I was obliged to do was when the salary was due, I would go and receive that salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the interview you said that there was a close family relation between Akif Sabic and Hilmo Selimovic who appointed him as the chief?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. This is not something that I know directly. I heard this story from my colleagues, from inspectors in the MUP who wanted to rush to give me the good news first, that they were actually very closely related.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then in your interview you said that with the arrival of Branko Kvesic at the head of the State Security Service, he, together with Zijo Rahimic on behalf of the SDA started to appoint their own people and to distribute equipment from the MUP depot only to those in the SDA and the HDZ, and in that way they started to dismantle the MUP. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me say right away -- let me explain it a little bit. You gave a very concise version and put a number of questions in one. First of all, Branko Kvesic became the head of the state security service and this other guy Zijo was working in the warehouse. He wasn't any kind of official but he had to be a person of confidence by the very nature of the work he was doing so that there wouldn't be any talk which organs were receiving which equipment in the field, was somebody being favoured, and somebody neglected. So in that sense they had to have confidence in this Zijo Rahimic. Not only Branko Kvesic, he was leader of the State Security Service, but also his immediate superior of Rahimic. This was the chief of the material and financial administration services, and that was Bruno Stojic who was from the HDZ and before the war he worked in Neum in the utility company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then was there reallocation of the resources of the MUP to the detriment of municipalities with a Serb majority?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I can assume that that was the case, and this is why -- here are the facts that can support that: All the way up until that point in time, that is to say, until Akif Sabic came to head the administration, I was I was absolutely aware of all the plans on the equipment and modernisation of all organs of the interior in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is to say that I directly authored some of these plans, and I was also in charge of the implementation of such a document. That was done in five-year intervals. The government would adopt such a document, financial document, then the Ministry of the Interior would define it in terms of its structure and in terms of the types of communications involved, then also the level of development of various municipalities was taken into account. There were six categories of municipalities, those that were the more developed ones, and then further on. I don't remember the exact names as to how they were defined. The very last category was the category of highly underdeveloped municipalities. So then this plan took all of that into account. The most developed ones, the most developed municipalities, financed 80 per cent of the equipment that they were entitled to, and the republic provided only 20 per cent, whereas in the last category, it was the other way around. The municipality itself would finance 20 per cent and the republic would finance 80 per cent. Of course, the proper administration took account of the actual equipment that was needed. I was the person who drafted this plan, and I was in charge of its implementation. When I, in that position, no longer saw these plans and had no further insight of what was being given to who, obviously it wasn't being done properly since they were hiding what they were doing, because why would you be hiding something that was right? You would hide something that is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the SDA brought Alija Delimustafic to head the MUP who had nothing whatsoever to do with the profession? He came from the business community. Not to mention that his brothers were operating on the very verge of lawfulness.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Alija Delimustafic, and that I know for sure -- actually, I'd have to remember which years were involved. He was assistant cook at the army centre in Sarajevo, and then he took a course for policemen, because every now and then these crash courses were organised for training such personnel. And then he started working as a policeman on the beat. Later on, I don't know how and according to what system, he established a company of his own, a trading company. It was probably -- how do I put this? He was not there all alone. He was part of a team that backed all of this up. The company was called Cenex, and then as such he came to head the MUP. It could not be said that he was qualified for that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember -- I think it's contained in your statements, that you were shown an intercept of a telephone conversation between me and Mr. Zepinic where I am asking why they want to transfer you to the Ministry of Defence. This shows that you and I do not know each other, because you remained in that position as an expert. Do you remember seeing that intercept?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I do. I do remember, and to tell you the truth, it was only from that text that I realised what was being discussed about me. No one every told me that I was supposed to be transferred to the Ministry of Defence or anywhere else in accordance with my professional background. I just know that I complained to Vito Zepinic, as deputy minister, about the attitude that was taken towards me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that also an attempt to remove you from the MUP and from the service where you matured and where you were an acting chief?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. That was one such attempt. There were quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether the SDS or Radovan Karadzic or any other party leader, apart from a demand to abide by the distribution of different posts among the different ethnic communities, did the SDS or Radovan Karadzic give any other orders to the police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive orders from the SDS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have agreed that the technical services for intercepts, et cetera, were taken up by the SDA and the HDZ.
