Do you know that from the very outset citizens' calls were being intercepted illegally, especially ethnic Serbs, and especially the SDS officials, and they were partners in government at the time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: As for the service that was involved in that, it was within the State Security Service, and it was located in the training centre of internal affairs in Vraca. If one looks at the personnel structure at the time, you will see that such work is carried out by Croats and Muslims; they are in charge of it. Now, if someone managed to do something apart from their superiors who were from those two groups, I don't know about it. Maybe there were such cases, but I don't think so. Perhaps it went the other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that this eavesdropping was for the benefit of the SDA and the HDZ, the other two partners in government?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, judging about how things developed generally speaking in terms of personnel policies and some lack of confidence which was developed as such and was on the rise within the Ministry of the Interior, and in other ministries the situation was not much butter. That I know from my contacts with colleagues elsewhere. It could be concluded that many things were being done apart from usual procedures, that is to say, that there was certain abuse of authority. That means that some people could abuse the fact that they have certain technical equipment in their hands. They could abuse it by not informing all of those who they should inform and not receiving all the approval that they should receive in order to do something like that. That is an assumption. As I've already said, a lot of stories were being bandied about. It was not exactly hearsay from the street. After all, there are quite a few people in this ministry, even those who belong to political parties, who were not exactly delighted by all of this, by doing away with the rules of service as such and by not doing things as they should be done in practice. A lot of these people were professionals, after all. They were a minority, truth to tell, but everything I heard from these people leads me to believe what they said, and I have no reason to doubt their truthfulness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned procedure. In order to intercept conversations of citizens, SDA -- SDS officials included, was it necessary to have official permission, and, if so, from whom?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: One had to receive a written order from the minister himself. Of course -- I mean, I don't want you to take this too literally. It's not that those people who were actually doing the bugging had to see the order themselves. Their supervisor would see the signed order and nothing could be done without that kind of signed order. Let me explain a milder form of this kind of work. On one day within my service in the telegraph and telephone department that I headed, a particular device appeared overnight, and I said, "What is this?" And they said, "Such and such a person is going to explain this to you." And he said to me, "This is a registering phone involving several channels, so it can record 10 or 20 different channels at a given point in time." So what was the task involved? And they said it was several telephone booths that were bugged, because there were provocations coming from these telephone booths. So we want to follow that. I don't know whether that was actually the case or not, so even though I was head of that department, I was not allowed to be part of this, and I was not familiar with all of details involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the minister issue this kind of order for listening in on conversations of citizens without a court order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I think it could not have been done without a court order. I'm saying it because I am not sure because that was not exactly my line of work, but the very logic of the situation would indicate that probably he had to issue an order on the basis of a court order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you as an expert in this field whether it is possible for intercepts to be changed, rigged, doctored in any way, both the recording and the transcript, by deleting parts of sentences or entire sentences?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: If you're asking whether it's possible technically, yes. The technical service is just one segment of this service, the ones who handle the actual equipment. Then there is the other service that listens to the recorded conversations and types up transcripts. So if it is in the hands of someone who is prepared to commit a violation and to abuse this in some way, of course they can do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your interview, you mentioned that you knew, that some Serb inspectors had told you about that, that Muslims and Croats from the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina were being sent to some training camps. They had recently been admitted, and then they were sent for training to camps in Croatia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about Croatia, but that certain personnel were sent to training camps, that is correct. However, I don't know which camps exactly and where all these camps were. That I don't know. However, I know that inspectors from the police administration went there as instructors. How should I put this? Everyone knew about it. A person would be gone for 15 days and then he'd come back and go away for another seven days, and then he'd come back to work, and that's how it went on, round and round in circles, so I think this had to do with the training of the reserve police. For the most part, it was the reserve police that was being trained, and perhaps the active-duty police to a lesser degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking or only from among the ranks of Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, that was the case. I didn't hear of Serbs going there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- or, rather, as for the representatives of the Croat ethnicity, the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina received for ethnic Croats various types of badges and other equipment that would show them as -- show them to be Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I did hear of that, so I could either die with that knowledge or -- or convey it further on. I heard about that from several people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Immediately after the elections in December 1990, at Sokolac, your house had burned down, however, you assume that that was the fault of a Serb; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. That is correct that the house burned down, and my friend, that is to say who worked in the service as an expert for arson, he's a personal friend of mine, he told me in confidence that all the material evidence indicates that this is a classical example of how the perpetrator of such a crime can be identified, that it was a case of arson, and then he explained how this happened, that floors can never move from one corner to the other unless some inflammable liquid was poured all over them and so on and so forth. Sokolac is an ethnic Serb area, so I don't see it could have been someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your interview with the OTP, 65 ter 22842, dated the 8th of November, 2004, on page 11, you described a bus that you took from Sokolac to go to work to Sarajevo was stopped at check-points of the Green Berets that checked people's IDs and asked the passengers whether they had any weapons. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. After the fire in my house, it was the month of December, so it was wintertime, right, we just managed to cover all of this with some kind of plastic sheets so that it wouldn't be even more damaged, and then we agreed -- we at home agreed that I would sleep in the house but at a lower level and that I would go to work every day by bus from Sokolac. So I went to work and I returned by bus to Sokolac, and I usually took the bus on the outskirts of town because it didn't really matter. Any bus that went to the east passed either through Sokolac or 3 or 4 kilometres in the direction of Romanija. So I used these buses for transportation, and I watched what was going on every single day. I saw it myself. They checked my IDs a countless number of times. They even asked me, "What's with you? We see you here every day." I invented all sorts of excuses. Sometimes, I actually told them the truth, that I was going home. Anyway, that was a fact. That went on every day and it went on for quite a while, as a matter of fact, from December when the fire took place in 1990 and then further on. Later on it happened more and more, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your Zupljanin/Stanisic evidence on page 107 in e-court, 1D3596, you confirmed that they even disarmed members of the MUP, the Green Berets that we mentioned, that they took their arms and checked their IDs, referring to MUP members who were not members of SDA. Was this Green Beret unit in any way authorised to perform these kinds of checks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was neither a legitimate nor authorised unit to do so. And I even heard from police inspectors, to make matters even worse, is that those who had uniforms, they had badges, inspector badges, and Muslims who returned home late at night from Sarajevo going to the outskirts, that they would be stopped and take their weapons, and they would even comment and say, "You know what? You're lucky you weren't slapped. I was slapped when they did that." So that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So even Muslims who were not members of the SDA were not spared; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't a member of the SDA, but I suppose so. They would probably know better anyway. But in any case, they had a grudge against regular police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your interview, in your statement, you also said that thanks to the kindness of a man from Tuzla, you got a list of Serbs who were slated for execution, and your name was pretty high up on that list, under number 4, and when you saw that on the eve of New Year of 1992, you left on vacation in order to hide yourself, in fact.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's correct. I was shown this by a JNA officer, and to be honest, I was so shocked by that I can't recall who the one, two, three, and five, and six and so on people were. It was so shocking that I just recall seeing my name under number 4 there. That was in late 1991 that I was shown this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the eve of New Year's Eve in 1992. Now, do you recall that in those days some prominent officers, primarily Serbs and people of other ethnicities, could observe that their apartments and their houses were marked by special symbols?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were numerous such instances. It was the case with homes of police officers but also of simple people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this strike fear into people's hearts or unease?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course. There were even cases. Well, there were even -- it was even possible to blow through the keyhole a -- some kind of gas that could either kill or disable a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In other words, after the war broke out, you were summoned by the minister and invited to come to Pale and to join the service in keeping with your experience and your expertise; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. He conveyed this message via his communications officer who was from Sokolac and who was working at the SJB, and he sent this message to me that I could -- that I should report to him for this purpose, and this happened in the very first days of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that for half a year or so you just sat there and you couldn't move anywhere other than around Pale and in that general area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's correct. When I was invited to go there, I went to Pale, to Karlovita Brda, to the Energoinvest building where I spent a few days. Then I received an order to go with a group of colleagues, chiefs of administrations and some other services to Vraca. We spent some time at Vraca, for as long as we could, but at one point in time it was no longer possible to stay there because there was a lot of sniping going around, and when they start shelling the area it became unbearable because this entire compound in Vraca was very open and vulnerable. There was nothing to protect it. Everything was aboveground. And I know that we would go to a kitchen that was underground to take a meal or so, and then we used some blankets and tents in order to try and build up some kind of screen in order to protect us. But when that became unbearable, we moved to Lukavica, and as a member of MUP at the headquarters, I remained there for a while, after which I returned to Pale, to the Kikinda facility, and only then did I get a bit more freedom of movement. I was even assigned a vehicle so I could move around, and then I started building up this system from scratch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you mention this fire being opened at Vraca, am I correct when I say that you could be targeted from -- from Zlatiste, Hum, Velesici, Pofalici, Zuc, Barino Brdo, Sokolje, and so on, so around 200 degrees around, Vraca was actually exposed to fire from all of these areas and this entire section?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: We I can tell you: Not 200 degrees, 360 degrees. We were exposed to fire from all areas. Because MUP had one building at Zlatiste that had been built for wartime purposes - this was built before the war - and I took part in the construction of that facility. Well, I had to do with the communication equipment. That was my involvement there. Now, when it was taken over from these people from the federation, Muslims - well, I don't want to say Muslim - Muslim units, part of the Special Unit of the Muslim federation, they all took up this facility. You also failed to mention Sanac, which is where they also took position. This was otherwise a neighbourhood where people from Sandzak lived. So they took position there, too, and opened fire from there as well. So whenever we went to Vraca, we would have to seek the cover of darkness in order to protect ourselves from the fire, from Sanac specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the government and the Presidency could not survive anywhere in the -- in the Sarajevo valley?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if the MUP could not survive there, I'm sure no one else could manage to stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at this -- during this period, as you said during your Zupljanin evidence, that's 1D3596, pages 19 and 20, you said that when you started this work, there was barely any infrastructure and that there were only two police officers, you and Zoran Borovcanin; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. He was the one who actually conveyed Mico's message to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how many men would it take to set up such a service and this -- without taking into account the loss of relay stations and so on? So how much time and how many men would it take to build up this kind of system?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the best way to answer this is to tell you that before the war my administration, which maintained all those communications stations and equipment, including the operators at the teleprinter centre, counted over 100 men, 100 staff, which means that in this situation, too, that number should not have been much lower, but we started off with just the two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The need for communications in wartime, is it comparable to the needs that the services have in war -- in peacetime?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in any way you look at it, it has to be greater. There has to be a greater need in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said in your Stanisic testimony, that's 13596, on pages 20, 22, 23, and 27, that while you were at Vraca, you did not have any phone lines with Pale and that by using mobile radio stations -- you could only use mobile radio stations, in fact, if there was electric power. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is correct, but I would like to explain that a bit further. The Vraca facility was connected to the republic SUP -- or, rather, MUP, with two cables. One was for public lines and the other one was for special lines, as we referred to them. In other words, police telephone lines and links to various police exchanges, because each police station had a telephone exchange, and it had as many connections as there were offices within it. Now, as soon as we moved into Vraca, this special cable was cut off from the main MUP building, and at the Dolac Malta telecommunications building, which we could see from Vraca, on orders from MUP the public cable was cut off as well, so that we were completely cut off. Later on, some police officers managed to obtain from their relatives or friends from their private homes, and they pulled two telephone cables to there, to the facility there in order to provide us with those -- these two phone lines. They were private phone lines from their homes. Now, as for the U -- the ultra shortwaves, there was radio waves, there was communication via a relay station, a repeater, and this was accessible to everyone, but there was no security provided and there could be no security provided on such open communication lines. Now, what happened without this repeater there was a direct link or communication between two -- if there was to be communication between two points, there would have to be visibility between them, but we would have to switch wavelengths all the time, but that, too, was no guarantee because any ham operator could actually be able to locate the frequency on which we would operate under such circumstances. Now, we also had shortwave stations, but as you know, such stations would have to have a special plan of work which would also provide for the time of communication, the wavelength and so on. So that, too, was practically useless. We did have one such device, but it was practically of no use.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the Trebevic relay saw frequent power shortages and that in wintertime you would have to carry oil, fuel, up there in through very high snow.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's true. The -- it was without power very frequently -- in the beginning it was on and off, but then at the end it was completely cut off. However, it did have a generator, but for the generator we needed fuel and that was a problem, because getting up to Trebevic, it was a difficult route that you had to actually negotiate on the way up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said that in the first few months you did not know who was holding what, because from Pale you couldn't get anywhere farther than Sokolac and that there was no communication between Banja Luka and Pale, so that in the first few days all communications and meaning here technical resources and various devices, all communication was for the most part local. Now, Mr. Gaynor pointed out, page 19 of the then transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I have a reference for the part that you've just road, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he's giving that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I think he's referring to today's transcript with page 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 19 of the then transcript. Could you give the reference, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first portion I related to the interview with the Defence. If it wasn't interpreted, my apologies. So, I just wanted the witness to confirm whether he actually said this to the Defence and then leading up to I'm going to ask him about Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now is this correct, as I've read it out from our interview, that there were no communications from Banja Luka and Pale, and that in the first few months you couldn't -- in the first few days, you couldn't move much further from Pale than Sokolac because nobody knew which territory was under what control?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, because this territory was completely unsafe. As you can see from the documents shown by the Prosecutor today, there were all the communications sent to those five CSBs via telephone. So it was possible to the teleprinter connection during those lines. However, in order to cover the information that also had to be protected -- or, rather, encrypted, there would have to be someone who would physically take these encryption codes and plans of work to all the participants in that network and on the first time it was me. At the time I went to Banja Luka it was the time when the corridor towards Brcko was broken through. I don't recall the exact dates but I know that I had to stay. I was stuck in Brcko for several days, and only a few days later somebody said, "Well, now you're free to go." And that was the first time I went to Banja Luka myself and discussed the problems that they had there, and, of course, the problems were more or less the same as everywhere else, however, the greatest problems would always be within the newly established bodies, because they had to start from scratch, including buildings, personnel, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today's transcript, on page 15, the log-book for Prijedor was shown. Is it correct that only dispatches received from neighbouring municipalities are shown there and none from eastern municipalities? Can we look at this log-book now. I failed to write down which P exhibit that is. 274. It was the first shown exhibit today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit P2744.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Can we please have P2744 in e-court. Do you agree, Mr. Kezunovic, can we look at the first page with the names of the municipalities -- or, actually, the CSBs or SJBs, if it's not here.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: What is on the screen here is before April 1992. That's the beginning of 1992. You can see in the second column the dates, 6th of January, 1992, onwards. This refers to the pre-war period before the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I any that this was not the first exhibit. The first exhibit, I think, was something else, and it referred only to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The first exhibit this witness dealt with is an order from Mr. Stanisic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The first exhibit that I showed the witness during the direct was the log-book from SJB Prijedor. It's not an order from Mr. Stanisic. The 65 ter number --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this was 16194A; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is what we are seeing now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please help me then to show what was received in Prijedor. Or it's a page in this document, but it's a bit further on. Page 20 in the Serbian and page 21 in the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From April on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Serbian page 20, English page 21. Would you agree that everything that was received by Prijedor was from its immediacy vicinity, Banja Luka, Bosnia Novi, and so on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: From what I can see on this page there's only Banja Luka, only in the first line we can see Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And were there wire connections there? Actually, Prijedor didn't receive anything from the headquarters, did it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, it did not. Prijedor, before the conflict broke out, was a security centre, and it covered Bosanski Novi, Sanski Most. Some four municipalities, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, Mr. Kezunovic: When we see a book, a log-book, that -- saying that something was received, can we take it definitely that this was actually received?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that we can, because how could it be recorded then at all, what was received or not? I mean, how else could it be other than that it was received?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But then when we see a log-book about what was dispatched, can we be sure that it actually arrived at its destination?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that would be a little more difficult. That does not have to indicate that. Perhaps it did and perhaps it didn't. Sometimes operators would tell the author of the document, the person sending the document, that it wasn't sent out because of such and such a reason. Sometimes it would send it out in five days' time. It doesn't matter what the degree of urgency was. If there were technical difficulties, then that's how it was. There were some cases that we looked at where the addressee would receive the document in five days, whereas at the other end from where it was being sent it would say that the dead-line to send the document would be six hours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The last two questions and answers were not translated because the speakers were too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Interpreters couldn't interpret the last conversation, but I note the time. If it is convenient, we'll take a break for half an hour and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that something was not completed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I do not know, so you can tell what was missed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was the last part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I may help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: There were two questions. The first one related to the incoming dispatches, whether what is written here would indicate that it was actually received, and I confirmed that. The second question referred to dispatches that were being handed in -- that were received. So did they actually arrive at their destination. And I said that it does not mean if it states so here that they were necessarily received at the other end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. My question was if they were handed in late, five or six days late, would the document still bear its old date?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Everything stays as in the original. Nothing is change -- changed. The operator possibly would write in by hand when it was actually delivered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Or would not do that, would not indicate it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Or would not indicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Do you agree that in view of the open lines and lack of coded documents the minister could not be informed about very delicate matters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I agree. It was always a question of - how shall I put it? - of to be or not to be in the dispatch traffic. Can we or can we not? So it was a matter of what at a certain point in time the availability of encryption would affect how something that was highly confidential would be sent out or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, people are reluctant to take the blame on themselves in front of the minister. Did the minister have the ability to send out an inspector to check whether the reports were correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know specifically, but he could have done that. I don't know whether he actually did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was communication easy, especially before the end of June, before the corridor was created?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't, not even on the Pale-Sokolac line. If you're thinking about physical communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I was thinking about the possibility of movement of an independent inspector to check whether the reports were accurate. Would he have difficulties reaching all these different destinations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your interview, you mention that even before the territorial links were established between certain regions in Republika Srpska, and after that communications or MUP connections depended to a large degree on the PTT telecom -- telecoms?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Karadzic. Is it that you want some reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, specifically, I would like Mr. Karadzic to clarify when he refers to the interview between himself, or rather, the Defence team, and Mr. Kezunovic and when he's referring to -- a copy of which the Prosecution does not have, we don't have any record of that interview - and the interview between the Prosecution and Mr. Kezunovic, and both parties have copies of that interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fair enough. Mr. Karadzic, are you referring to your interview, your meeting with the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said in the interview with the Defence, but with the Defence it was not recorded, either because I'm speaking fast or either because I am not enunciating it correctly. If it had been an interview with the Prosecution, I would have given the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Kezunovic, do you still remember the question, or shall I ask him to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would like the question to be repeated, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wanted to say whether it was correct about what you told us in the interview, that before territorial links were established between certain regions of Republika Srpska and after that the situation with the communications to a large degree depended on the situation with the PTT network.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: As far as written and spoken messages were concerned, that exclusively depended on PTT telecommunications, because everything relied on that. So depending on the situation of the general system or system in certain areas, we always depended on -- on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We noticed in reports that often a report from Trebinje was missing. That is covering the whole the Eastern Herzegovina. Is it correct that communications with Trebinje proceeded via Montenegro and that we depended on the goodwill of an operator over there who was running the communications system?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That system was modified and turned towards Montenegro and linked up to some node in Montenegro. So I think that even the numbers of Trebinje and all the connections began with the Montenegro area code.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that there were such problems with repairs. There was a shortage of cable or wire or equipment, or there was a shortage of qualified staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were short of everything, material, instruments, tools, workers, especially workers with experience. For example, 50 per cent of our technical personnel were without any experience at all of working in the police system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you say that in this interview with the Defence, the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of the Interior often faced identical problems, because they both depended on the telecommunications system; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely. I think our problems were very similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You spoke about encryption. This is 1D5396, testimony in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case, pages 116 and 117. Stating that the MUP had internal regulations regarding the type of documents which could be communicated in open lines. The criteria was based on the confidentiality and importance of the data; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were instructions drafted describing all the possible situations regarding contents so that the author could correctly determine the degree of confidentiality and urgency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned today that you physically had to take the documents and the encryption things, and in the pages in the Zupljanin and Stanisic case, 121 and 122, the encryption codes would expire so that new ones had to be taken over physically.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: The code books had a certain period of validity. When they expired, they had to be replaced, and this had to be organised in time so that there would be no interruption, because new documents failed to arrive. However, there were some extraordinary situations as well. The rules on keeping documents were very rigorous so that sometimes it would happen that one of the articles defining events in which the secrecy of the code book was violated. Even if it was suspected that something like that happened, even if we didn't have specific data that the document was compromised, we would be suspicious. Somebody would try to open it, perhaps, and perhaps by mistake the encryption operator would take out the wrong book and then he wouldn't be able to admit that he actually did it, but if even there was a suspicion of somebody violating the confidentiality of the code book it had to be replaced, which involved additional time, additional complications, expenses, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your interview with the Prosecutor, that is 65 ter number 22482, on page 26 and 30, and in your testimony in Stanisic and Zupljanin, 1D3596 on page 118, you said that there was shortwave communication but that it was limited and it wasn't sufficient for sending longer messages or written messages; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain it briefly why that was the case. Not all organs had the possibility, especially in the beginning, of this machine encoding. That is to say that there is a device that produces coded text as fast as possible, and then it would be transmitted via shortwave radio. It actually had to be done manually, so it was a slow procedure and rather complicated at that. We tried to transmit only the shortest dispatches via that system, only those consisting of a few sentences. However, we tried to keep it going for the sake of practice, as it were. We established connections, and we established what the quality of the connection was, but it was possible to communicate via that system as well. Now, how long it would take depended on the individual case involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this interview 65 ter 22482, on page 33 you say that communications could go via radio relay stations that were on mountaintops and through cables on the ground, and you say that it was easy to cut cables when they passed through enemy territory. Was it easy to cut cables that went close to the separation lines?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was possible. It was possible. In practice, there were all sorts of situations. However, more often it was the relay stations that were under attack quite simply by virtue of their physical position. They are more exposed to artillery fire. Quite simply, as soon as somebody cuts your power off, everything else becomes useless. They don't need to do anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the same interview, on page 30 you said that radio communication largely depended on weather conditions, and in poor weather conditions, waves could not reach the receiving party; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that pertains to shortwave radio stations. When work plans are elaborated, then different weather forecasts have to be taken into account, geomagnetic ones as well and others, so that at a given point in time a proper range would be selected that would be least susceptible to atmospheric conditions. Since we could not use this kind of forecast at the time, we worked out these plans of frequency selection approximately. Sometimes it was simply impossible to establish any communication through the frequencies selected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Stanisic/Zupljanin on pages 35 and 112, you said that there was a courier service but that its limitations were the lack of vehicles and manpower for this to be able to function; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Officially this courier service was established only, I think in 1993, perhaps even in 1994. And I was actually the one who insisted on it the most, because these different centres were under such great pressure with regard to documents that were not urgent at all. As a matter of fact, we were wasting resources, the code books and the paper and the equipment we had, and the special paper for telefaxes and teleprinters, et cetera. Then they embarked on this organisation. They decide it had would be within the duty service. So I'm saying "they," because I was not involved. Then the area was visited. They had vehicles at their disposal. You know what it was like. They collected things from different centres, and then the couriers would go to different centres. They would then distribute whatever was there, and that's how it functioned during a certain period of time until there were no more resources left starting with vehicles, fuel, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the proximity of the front line another factor that worked against this, also the fact that the territory was all split up? Would couriers sometimes actually get killed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, but these official couriers who work -- who worked on such jobs and all other members the service who went out on the ground were asked by other persons to carry some mail. That would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the chief of the security centre of the Sarajevo Romanija region, Zoran Cvijetic, got killed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As he was travelling by car?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Stanisic/Zupljanin on page 176 you said that the MUP did not dare use a fax because these messages could not be coded. And on pages 103 through 126, you say in relation to a letter sent by Predrag Jesuric, you say that he said in that letter that there was no communication between Bijeljina and Pale, and you said in that testimony that you believe that was mainly due to power cuts.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I think that that was the main reason, and that's what I said in some of my previous statements. I confirm that. When I was transferred to Bijeljina, I saw for myself that a countless number of times, 50 times during a single day there would be no power. As for the death of couriers, an engineer who worked in communications and was then transferred to state security communications and a technician who accompanied him, they were killed at Crni Vrh.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Stanisic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Interpreters noted that they did not hear the end of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Crni Vrh and Caparde. That's the only thing that's missing. Crni Vrh is in the area of Caparde; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Caparde.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: C-a-p-a-r-d-e.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you mention that Caparde was the only area that allowed for communication, because the Muslims held Konjevic Polje and the area between Vlasenica and Zvornik and as for this only road that was functioning they had ambushes even there and were killing civilians. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. These two men got killed on that road. And it wasn't only the two of them. They were in a column, and it was ambushed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I see that that's what you confirmed on pages 131 and 132 in Stanisic/Zupljanin. 3596 is the e-court reference, 1D, that is. During that testimony, also on page 129, you confirmed -- actually, they showed you a letter that shows that between Pale and Sarajevo there were major problems in terms of communication, and that's only about 15 kilometres; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. There were two roads across Trebevic that was constantly under sniper fire and other fire, and also another one around Jahorina and I can't remember now, Tilava. Yes, yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you testified in Stanisic/Zupljanin pages 164 and 165 in e-court you give your comments on reports of the CSB Banja Luka and these reports say that telephone and telefax lines were interrupted and that that led to chaos in the communications system. Also, that from the beginning of the war, 50 per cent of all telegrams were sent in the Banja Luka region, and you say -- or you said to us in the interview that this situation was even worse. That's later; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. That situation was created by intentional cuts in Sarajevo, in the MUP of the BH. That is to say all communications from the centres led to the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the centre in Sarajevo. And it was the easiest to switch off equipment there. You didn't have to destroy anything. You simply unplugged something. You take part of the device out and that's it; an entire communication line is down in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very often regionalisation and how justified or unjustified it was has been discussed here. I don't want to go into that, but you will note this from the professional point of view, from the point of view of your very own profession. Am I right if I say that all the Eastern Herzegovina were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Mr. Karadzic will have to start again. This is too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you're speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So Serb areas, Eastern Herzegovina were linked to Mostar and depended on Mostar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Serb areas in Old Herzegovina were linked to Gorazde where 30 per cent were Serbs and 70 per cent were Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Serb areas around Sarajevo linked to the centre of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Serb parts of Semberija and Posavina were linked to Tuzla; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: And also Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, Zvornik was also linked to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Bratunac, Srebrenica, Vlasenica, that entire eastern area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Serb part of Posavina and Doboj and Ozren were linked to Zenica; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Part to Zenica and part to Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And Visoka Krajina, that is to say Drvar, there was 100 per cent Serb; and then Grahovo, predominantly Serb, over 90 per cent; Glamoc, 11 per cent were non-Serbs; Petrovac, and so on, they were linked to Bihac; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Part of them to Bihac and part to Livno as a pre-war centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Neither Bihac nor Livno were predominantly Serb-populated territory; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So with the exception of Banja Luka, all other Serb areas were linked to centres where the SDA or the HDZ were in power; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And what I mentioned a moment ago was the reason for the damage sustained. Nobody had to destroy stations or cut lines along roads. They could simply unplug all of this at the various centres without any destruction whatsoever and later they could simply plug all of this back in when they needed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they do that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in your testimony in Stanisic/Zupljanin, that is 1D3596 on page 161, that on average there were about 300.000 dispatches per year before the war. That is to say about 22.000 per month going through the communications centre of the MUP in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 162 and page 163, you said that after the war broke out in Republika Srpska that covered 70 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, during the first nine months of the war there were about 8.500 dispatches, and that was due to poor communication. You didn't say that there, actually, that that was because of poor communication. Wasn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That is what was written in the report, the report on the work involved where all the results were brought together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Today you confirmed that most of these dispatches were open rather than coded and that when the war broke out there was increased need for dispatches and the number was actually brought down to some 10 per cent; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, because that reflects the situation of communications, the actual state of the communications involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the interview with the Defence, you confirmed that from time to time you did attend, not always, that you attended collegium meetings but that you attended one meeting when Mr. Stanisic, the minister, was shouting at the police and calling for the arrest of the Yellow Wasps, although this was a risky and difficult operation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Further on -- actually, can I summarise now the ways in which communications went down. First of all, most of the nodes remained under control of the Muslims and Croats, especially those in mountains and in centres.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The main communications centre in Dolac Malta and Mostar, Tuzla, Zenica, Bihac, and so on; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. And in appropriate units, organisational units in the MUP. That is to say that in each and every one of these centres that is where the final -- that's where the lines ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Especially in newly established municipalities and also the existing ones there were many shortcomings. There wasn't enough equipment, and there weren't enough trained people; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The repairs to the communication routes close to the front lines suffered damage in combat, but also it was risky because of fire that was -- and the fighting that was going on there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The severing of cables, that was something that was done in sabotage operations; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There was also a problem with power shortages as well as fuel shortages, fuel that was needed for generators.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Also, there was a shortage in spare parts for these generators, not just fuel, because every 15 hours or so, I believe, these generators had to be updated. Some parts had to be replaced. So that, too, was a problem. And I believe that we broke all records in our work under such conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there also a shortage of spare parts for telecommunications equipment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course, like for everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We do not have a map ready today, and I will ask you tomorrow to mark the various nodes or hubs of communication, but for now I would request 65 ter 30888. 30088.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Admitted as Exhibit D364, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. Thank you. Could we now have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here where we see Zepinic says -- could we have the same page in Serbian as well. In the middle approximately it says, or I say: "We should take a position." Do you recall that this was an intercept of a conversation between me and Zepinic on the 24th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And I see here it says I'm supposed to sign something. Simovic signs something for Kezunovic, a man I don't know but what we know is that it's coming from the MUP, from the Ministry of Defence. Is this what we were talking about a little earlier, an attempt to remove you from the MUP?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Excuse me. The record we have is that the conversation took place on 24th July, 1991, not 1992. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did say 1991, but never mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the same page it says, Zepinic says that it's important that that position at the Ministry of Defence is important and then I ask, "Well, do you know this man?" Can we have the next page. He says, "Well, this morning he same to see me," and so on and so forth. The next page, please. And then here I say, "Well, no. Let him -- let Kezunovic stay where he is if that's of interest to us. He shouldn't be moved without our approval. What Hilmo is doing or what Alija is doing or whoever else, the basic thing is they should never again --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Probably the next page for English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please see in Serbian this part. I won't read any more. So do you agree that what I am saying here is that Serbian staff that are appointed should be appointed by Serbs and not by Hilmo or Alija? Do you agree? Is that what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now have 65 ter 1505, please. 65 ter 01505.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Admitted as Exhibit P2768, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, apparently there's nothing I can offer as an exhibit that Mr. Gaynor hadn't already done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, here we see on the first page that you attended a meeting of the professional collegium on the 14th of April, 1992, and then this paragraph 3 it says: "There is a gap between Pale and the Serbian MUP ..." And then a bit further down it says: "People move in a disorderly fashion or without any official badge within the MUP premises." Can we have the next page, please. The next page where it says "Dragan Kezunovic." "Dragan Kezunovic: We don't have a sufficient number of men at -- in the communications department. Only three men applied. We should provide resources, staff, and so on. We have major problems with communications in the field and maintaining links with other structures." That's what you were talking about a little earlier; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have 65 ter 11527, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is Exhibit P2758.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph, it says: "Because of problems with communication, the above-mentioned centres must inform all SJBs in their territory of the concerns of this dispatch." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now have 1D3597, please. I believe that Mr. Gaynor has already used this. It's dated the 18th of April, and it's a request for a daily report. So we don't have to look at that. Can we have 18366, 18366. The earlier document has already been admitted into evidence. It was tendered by Mr. Gaynor. So 65 ter 18366, please. Would you agree that it says here: "We warn you once again --" Minister Stanisic says, on the 20th of April: "I'm warning you again that you're obliged to submit a bulletin of daily events everyday ..." And so on and so forth. So this shows that there were certain difficulties; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have 1D3598, please. 1D3598, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you are tendering the previous document, are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly. I thought that Mr. Gaynor had already tendered it. He hasn't? Well, could I tender it then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That would be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1363, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that this is a dispatch from the Minister of the Interior, Stanisic, to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Montenegro where he requests that communications with Trebinje be enabled?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1364, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have 1D3599, please. I don't know if we have a translation. Yes, we do. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree here that Minister Stanisic is requesting information on the resources at the disposal of the centres of the republic -- Republika Srpska MUP? So this is sent to all SJBs in the Sarajevo area. In other words, not even in Sarajevo at this time did he know what resources were at the disposal of the SJBs; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1365, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 65 ter 07502, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit P2763, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the first paragraph of this communication from Mr. Jesuric, the chief of the Bijeljina CSB, addressed to the minister, the minister of the interior, and he says: "Due to a breakdown in the telephone, telegraph, and fax communications, during the period from the last report you did not receive any reports, although they were compiled by the chief of the Bijeljina CSB." Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Correct. Perhaps this is a good time for me to repeat what I said earlier. As far as the system that was in use by the Ministry of Interior - and I am referring to all types of communication equipment - in the period before the conflict broke out, all towns except Banja Luka and Doboj, in other words, all the communications centres, nodes where the communications could be manipulated or plugged or unplugged, they were all on the other side. In other words, the opposing side had all the possibilities to plug or unplug anything, any mode of communication, not to mention all the resources that the MUP had in Sarajevo and what all equipment and devices our side could not use, whereas they could because it had remained in their territory regardless of where those cables and wires ran, through what territory. And regardless of what cables and wires we had in town. So all of our difficulties -- or our disadvantages were their advantages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I will ask you to mention -- to mark these nodes and the relay stations on elevations tomorrow. Now, could we please have 1D00668.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, just one question. How late are we working today, to 2.30?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we have 65 ter 00668, please. 65 ter 00668, please. Unless Mr. Gaynor beat me to it here too.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is P2764, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here the Zvornik SJB, public security station, we can see that on page 1, is complaining about the emergence of these paramilitary units, but can we have page 3. There's a portion I would like to refer you to. This is page 2. Can we have page 2 now, please. Or, rather, we can stay here. The difficulties at the very top. The difficulties in work -- we have another difficulty in the work. It's called by the system of communications between the reserve police station and the neighbouring municipalities. And then a little lower down, a little further down in the same paragraph it says: "We also lack other technical equipment such as means for carrying out on-site investigations of car accidents and crimes." And then further down the third paragraph from the bottom, it says that communications should be established with the army and other organs. Now, does it say here that there was no communication even with police stations in their own areas, let alone the neighbouring municipalities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: My apologies. Can you just tell me where this document is coming from?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, can we have the first page. This is the Zvornik MUP, the public security station in Zvornik. We need the page before this one in Serbian. Now we need the next page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a report on the situation in Zvornik public security -- in the Zvornik Public Security Station, that's correct. They couldn't even maintain communication with their reserve stations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] can we now have 65 ter 00793, please. Maybe this one was -- has already been admitted too, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2762, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't have to call it up. Now you remember that Mr. Gaynor asked you here -- he referred you to the place where it says that CSBs Bijeljina --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have 1D3600, please. [In English] It's admitted already, no? [Interpretation] 1D3600. Do you agree that on the 20th of May the minister is writing to all the CSB centres and states: In order to monitor the status of organisations, personnel, replenishment and other elements in the police command and control system, it is required that you submit the following information broken down by public security station and then there is a list of data required by the minister, and in the last number it states data is to be provided by messenger by the 5th of June, 1992, at the latest. Do you remember that the corridor was not broken through until the 28th of June, 1992, until St. Vitus Day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I recall it wasn't broken through at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you can we admit this please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I don't think that one's already been tendered. No objection to its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1366, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have P39 here. I don't know if we should call it up or should I just ask you -- well, let's call it up, P39, so you can just look at it. P39?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told that this is a document under seal, so we need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see any reason for that. I don't see why it would be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In any event, if we don't broadcast this document, I think we can remain in public session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please see if this is a dispatch by the minister of the 17th of June asking for assessments to be provided, and in the middle it says incidents of looting and war profiteering and other severe crimes that have an affect on the state of security and so on and so forth. Can we conclude on the basis of this that it is not essential to report on any lighter, less serious crime, but he is asking for reports of more serious crimes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's probably so. For the purposes of statistics, it's necessary to report back urgently. Not about every single crime that occurs, but only those grave ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last sentence says that it should be submitted by the courier, by the dead-line. Does that mean that the secure connection is not operating on the 17th of July either?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Most probably, since in the beginning he already stated the manner in which it should be delivered, and probably these are quite detailed information describing the crimes which would bottle up the system. It would become blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And at the bottom it says "Failure to respect the order shall be deemed a severe violation of work duty," so-and-so and then there is a signature at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. And this is what he insisted on all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we please know why this would be something under seal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was the question I was want -- about -- I was considering. Shall we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D3601 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the document of the 1st of October, 1992. It's an activity report of the communications and cryptographic data protection department for the period from 30th of July to 30th of September, 1992, for the Doboj CSB. Does this document speak of the difficulties in setting up communications, in disruptions, depending on the combat and so on and so forth? Can you please briefly tell us about the problems. Well, here is the end of the second paragraph: "Frequent disruptions in the communications with Maglaj and Petrovo due to the damage caused by intensive war activities."

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what that is. We've been talking about it the whole time. First of all, there was the problem in the direction towards the MUP and then also along the lines of the subordinated police station. So the problems spread upwards and downwards, hierarchically speaking, and this is a brief description of it. It was our practice to speak about it in much more detail, but there was no need to put all of that in in the reports, to speak specifically of the problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this was the situation at the end of September. The report is dated the 1st of October, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1367, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 18452. This has already been admitted; right?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2760.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at the second page, please. Second page in the Serbian. In the English I think that it's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see that towards the end of the first paragraph in the middle it says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have the reference in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you give the reference from which you are reading in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's this page. It's the end of the second paragraph. [In English] "Problems in providing material and technical ..." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In addition, there were initially hardly any records, crime investigation technical equipment, communications equipment, et cetera, which is all essential for the quality of work, especially in the case of internal affairs organs. Does this correspond to your experience?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And this is the gist. This is a conclusion pertaining to all of those questions. Simply it puts all of the problems clearly into one sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at page 5 in the Serbian, please. It bears 4 as the page number, but I think it's actually the fifth page. 6796 is the ERN number. One page further in the Serbian. I think in the English we're all right for the beginning, and then we can turn the page. "Duties and tasks of the public security service." It states here -- yes, this part in the English is okay. Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic, crime fighting department, I'm skipping some things.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: This is too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With this speed, the interpreters can't follow you simply.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the following page in the English. It should be at the end of 6796.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But again I'm repeating, Mr. Karadzic. You don't have to read all the sentences. You can just summarise and put the question, and then we can read the documents later on. If the witness can't follow, then you can read them. Proceed, Mr. Karadzic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These two paragraphs are actually the first paragraph beneath the tasks and assignments of the National Security Service. Do they indicate that before the war broke out the Serb cadres were decimated, replaced, retired off, dismissed from work and that the service cleansed in such a way was in the service of the policy of the SDA and the HDZ and that SDS leaders, members of the JNA, prominent Serbs were followed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the English, it should be National Security Service, and I don't see that in the English. I apologise. It's my mistake for not indicating the pages in the English. Can we look at page 8 in the Serbian and page 6 in the English. Well, this was the duties and task of the public security service. A little bit earlier it was the national -- nations and that document was already adopted, and it says: "According to information available to the ministry, and they're not complete because of the bad communication systems with certain security services centres in the Srpska Republika ..." Does that confirm that the communications were bad?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have the next page in the Serbian and in the English we can stay on this page for a while, this page 6. The first paragraph speaks about the number of submitted criminal reports and then the next one talks about that there is data about war crimes and other crimes and that it -- they are being documented. I am not reading now. I am putting the question. I'm paraphrasing. Thus, do you agree that the first paragraph indicates that criminal charges were entered against 24 persons and everything is being documented including war crimes? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the third paragraph it is stated that a greater degree of linking in is required, especially regarding war crimes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the degree of effort invested by the MUP in order to update the communications systems between the MUP and the CSBs? Was everything done that could be done?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Everything that could have been done was done. Everything that we were able to think of and within the means that we had at our disposal. Let me just say this: It's much easier when you start making something from scratch and you have a normal situation, but it's very difficult but when you are in the position of practically reconstructing something. Even the things that were supposed to operate in the territory in which Serbs were -- could not function because the most crucial and most important elements were switched off in those communications centres, in the buildings and MUP organs, and these were the telecoms which were the main bearer and it was the infrastructure that the MUP used. So it was very difficult in those circumstances, because that does not only depend on whether you know how to build something but how to combat these persistent actions by the opposing side. Hopefully, I was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that the sanctions imposed on Yugoslavia and Republika Srpska interfered with the procurement of up-to-date equipment and spare parts for old equipment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. And it wasn't just that. This was also subject to procurement of spare parts and other materials. It's not just specialised equipment that was under special regime but also paper was a part of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paper as subject to restrictions. Can we have page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter kindly asks the accused to repeat the page numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the page number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 11 in the Serbian, 7 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Duties and tasks related to communications and cryptographic protection." And then the second part of the sentence states: "Resulted in the total collapse of all communications systems of the former MUP due to either physical damage and destruction or deliberate shutdowns by the former MUP." "For instance, special telephone links -- can we have the following page in the Serbian, the following page in the Serbian, please. Special telephone links, teleprinter links and cryptographic protection systems were either destroyed or shut down." let me not read any further. So is this what your experience is and what you know of these matters and this is on the 29th of June, 1992? That is the date of the report.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is what we spoke about earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
