utterances.text: Can we just have page 8 in English, please. Does it say here the shortwave and ultra shortwave radio networks used by internal affairs organs are also falling apart? And then further down it says that in newly formed security centres there is also a shortage of these material and in Serbian, and I believe in English as well, it says that electronic jamming is also present in this system, and it says, Some of our participants in these communications engage in futile quarrels with the enemy through this system, thus rendering it inoperative.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: The last bit was characteristic of all parties in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So there was electronic jamming as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since this document was admitted, can we just have page 14 in Serbian and 9 in English to see what was situation was with regard to providing information about difficulties. This is what it says here, right, that CSBs and public security stations informed -- I'm actually not reading; I'm just speaking about this. It depended on the quality of communications and other circumstances. Can we have the next page in Serbian. Is it right as is written here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The next page in Serbian, the second paragraph, to inform top officials, basically the minister and the prime minister, a daily bulletin was being issued. Sixty came out until now. Do you agree that the Presidency and the Assembly did not have to be rapported [as interpreted] on daily matters, except if something dramatic happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I agree. That was not within my own line of work, so I did not have any influence there. It's not that I provided any opinions of my own at that point, but I fully agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here that basically this is being sent to the minister and the prime minister; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since the document has been admitted, we're not going to waste any time. Let's just find this. 65 ter 11241.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit P2761, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously the Prosecution was very hard-working. Can we have -- I see this is the report on the period for April/December 1992, that is to say all of the war year of 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 31 in e-court in Serbian, please, and 22 in English, e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this says that there is a lack of operative records and there are difficulties in communication due to war operations, that there is a shortage of personnel and so on and so forth, and these were all difficulties that affected proper information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: I agree, especially in the operative services, because that's what they were called, operative records from different fields; crime prevention, public law and order, and various other things that were part of the work of the Ministry of the Interior. So then you have systems of persons and -- and crimes that were committed, particular cases that were being solved, and so on. And if you have no knowledge from earlier on, you have no records of perpetrators from earlier on, of course it's more difficult to work under such circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that information that is important for the security of the country would have to be submitted to the president -- or, rather, the Presidency of the republic so that this could be shared with the military, whereas as far as crime is concerned, the president doesn't need to be informed about that if work is being done about that already?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thirty-six in Serbian, 25 in English. Could we have those pages now please. "Tasks and duties of communications and cryptographic data protection." Do you agree that it refers to three basic elements of work in communication and cryptographic data protection; personnel, technical equipment and documents, and that at first most of the problems were in those areas? And also in nine -- also that nine centres, those nodes that you refer to are -- are in the former centres of security. In our hands, we only had the CSB Banja Luka and the CSB Doboj and the nodes within them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And also the cryptographic data protection system broke down, et cetera, et cetera. Then the system of radio communications was also falling apart.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. So this has already been admitted we're not going to dwell on it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 05511, could we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Exhibit P2766, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we then have -- actually, I believe it's number 18 in e-court. The ERN number is 0324-6781. Yes, that's it in Serbian. And in English may God help us. 671. Other tasks. Do you agree that the Banja Luka centre is providing information here to the effect that they do not have enough professionals and not enough vehicles and fuel and towards the bottom it says that what has been received is 728 confidential dispatches? Is this about 10 per cent of what the situation was before the war, and was the Banja Luka centre in a better position compared to the public security stations that were around it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was better off in relation to the other centres, but also in it's area it had newly established stations that had started from scratch as well. However, this is a report of the 1st of January. That is to say, before the outbreak of the armed conflict and then up until the 30th of June, so most of it refers to the time before the outbreak of the conflict. So these figures are not very relevant for the period during war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's three months before the war broke out and three months after the war broke out; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And the Banja Luka centre was a focal point for dispatches for Livno, Doboj and Prijedor. That is to say, it covered a territory that was much larger, technically speaking, than the centre covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the one-but-last page in Serbian, and I believe that's the way it is in English too. The penultimate one in Serbian and in English too. It says, "The engagement of organs." So one page back in Serbian and in English. You see that part where it says that in Bosanska Krajina, in the war-ravaged part of Bosnia-Herzegovina actually various phenomena or described, and if these tendency continue in the coming period, it is realistic to expect a deterioration in the actual situation and it would be unrealistic to expect self-organisation in terms of government. And then further on it says terror and violence against the population, grave forms of crime and general anarchy. Can we move on to the next page in both languages? So is this in line with your own experience and knowledge and the capabilities of our MUP at the time and their ability to introduce law and order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC
utterances.text: Everywhere the situation was more or less the same like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be it for today. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are seized of two motions, one related to upcoming witness Nebojsa Ristic, and the other a protected witness about whose protective measures the Defence is challenging. Could we expect some expedited responses from the Prosecution, given that they are coming very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We're aiming at with respect to the first an expedited response by -- hopefully by close of business tomorrow. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We may be talking about two different things. One response has already been filed that you haven't received, so I misspoke, and I think we're even faster than I might have hoped. I also wanted to respond to the Court's inquiry earlier this morning concerning the motion for access in the Dragomir Milosevic case, and first I wanted to apologise to the Court for the oversight, but more substantively, I wanted to indicate to the Court that there will be no objection and that the OTP will co-ordinate with the Registry to identify any documents subject to Rule 70 protections that may require consent of the provider in order to disclose in other cases such as this one. And we are willing to assist the Registry in -- in obtaining such consent in those cases where the exhibit was provided initially to the Defence by the Prosecution, but, of course, we are not in a position to know about or address conditions for documents submitted by the Defence for documents that didn't originate with the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Tieger. We will rise for today. Tomorrow, 9.00 in the morning.
